topic.title: The wedding loan the younger sibling inherits
topic.claim: A wedding loan doesn't end when the shehnai stops, it quietly becomes the next sibling's EMI, and we call that family duty.
topic.behaviour: Parents borrow heavily to give each daughter a grand wedding. The earning son or sibling is left worrying about repayment and can't say it out loud without sounding selfish.
topic.mechanism: A wedding works as the parents' public report card on duty and love. Debt is hidden inside that, so questioning the budget feels like questioning the love. The cost is passed to whoever earns next.
topic.group: metro and small-city millennials and Gen Z who are the earning child in the family

sources.fact: The WedMeGood 2025 report found about 15% of couples took wedding loans, with an average loan of Rs 15.5 lakh against an average all-India wedding budget of Rs 39.5 lakh.
sources.excerpt: around 79 per cent of couples funded their weddings through their savings, while just 15 per cent took loans. The average loan size stood at Rs 15.5 lakh. The all-India average budget for a wedding reached Rs 39.5 lakh.

sources.fact: Zerodha Varsity says wedding debt often passes to the bride's father and brother, and cites IndiaLends surveys showing marriage as a large share of loans among young Indians.
sources.excerpt: The girl's father and brother will repay the loan. It does not impact the newly wedded couple. 20% of all loan applications received from young Indians aged 20-30 years in 2018-19 were for marriage. the average ticket size for marriage loans was the highest at ₹4.13 lakh. The longing to create one dreamy, colossal day could cripple your personal finance for years to come.

paragraphs: Papa earns ₹30,000 a month and retires next year. The second sister's wedding costs ₹20 lakh. So whose salary is paying for it?
Zerodha Varsity says it plainly: the debt often falls on the bride's father and brother.
The couple goes on the honeymoon. The EMI stays home.
Second sister's wedding, around ₹20 lakh. A ₹10-15 lakh loan planned. About ₹4 lakh unpaid from the first sister's.
Papa earns about ₹30,000 a month and retires in a year. The earning kid makes about ₹58,000.
In a year, papa's salary stops. The old ₹4 lakh and the new loan don't.
There's exactly one salary left in the house, and everyone at the dinner table knows whose.
And the kid can't really say it.
Asking for a smaller wedding sounds like loving your sister less. Mention a postponement and you're the selfish one by dinner.
So you nod, and open the EMI calculator later.
Because the wedding is papa's report card. A full shaadi hall is the grade.
The loan is the part of the report card nobody prints. It just gets handed to the kid.
Look at the family photo from the sister's wedding.
The one paying for it is standing at the edge, smiling.

draft.caption: If you're the earning kid, which family wedding are you still paying for?
draft.alt_text: A seven-slide text carousel about how wedding loans in Indian families often pass to the earning son or sibling. It walks through a typical case: a second sister's wedding around ₹20 lakh, a planned ₹10-15 lakh loan, ₹4 lakh left from the first wedding, and a father earning ₹30,000 who retires in a year while the child earns ₹58,000. It argues that the wedding works as the parents' public report card, so questioning the budget feels like questioning love, and the debt lands on the next earner.

hook_candidates.hook: Papa earns ₹30,000 a month and retires next year. The second sister's wedding costs ₹20 lakh. So whose salary is paying for it?
In a lot of Indian homes, the wedding loan gets passed down to the next kid. Like the family jewellery, but worse.
Look at any big Indian wedding photo. Somewhere at the edge, smiling, is the person who'll be paying for it long after the honeymoon.
We say the whole family pays for a wedding. Usually it's one kid's salary, and nobody at the dinner table says it out loud.
The couple goes on the honeymoon. The EMI stays home. And it's looking for the next kid with a salary.
